content: 1. Brentuximab vedotin metabolism is influenced by the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Exercise caution and monitor therapy when co-administered with grapefruit or CYP3A4 inhibitors. 2. Grapefruit increases guanfacine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors significantly elevate guanfacine plasma concentrations. For extended-release guanfacine, the FDA recommends halving the dose if co-administered with CYP3A4 inhibitors. No specific recommendations exist for immediate-release guanfacine. 3. Grapefruit increases hydrocodone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is essential. Co-administration with CYP3A4 inhibitors may elevate hydrocodone plasma concentrations, potentially leading to fatal respiratory depression. 4. Grapefruit increases hydrocortisone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 5. Grapefruit increases hydroxyprogesterone caproate levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 6. Grapefruit decreases ifosfamide levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Co-administration with CYP3A4 inhibitors may reduce the metabolism of ifosfamide to its active alkylating metabolites, decreasing its efficacy. 7. Grapefruit increases iloperidone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 8. Grapefruit increases imipramine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 9. Grapefruit increases indinavir levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 10. Grapefruit increases ixabepilone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 11. Grapefruit increases ketamine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 12. Grapefruit decreases ketoconazole levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor therapy. 13. Grapefruit increases lapatinib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 14. Grapefruit decreases levoketoconazole levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor therapy. 15. Grapefruit increases levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol/ferrous bisglycinate levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Co-administration with CYP3A4 inhibitors may elevate plasma hormone concentrations. Nonhormonal contraceptive use is recommended. 16. Grapefruit increases lopinavir levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 17. Grapefruit increases loratadine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 18. Grapefruit increases lumacaftor/ivacaftor levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Due to lumacaftor's CYP3A induction effect, ivacaftor exposure at steady state is not expected to exceed monotherapy levels. No dose adjustment is needed when CYP3A inhibitors are initiated in patients already on lumacaftor/ivacaftor. However, when starting lumacaftor/ivacaftor in patients on strong CYP3A inhibitors, reduce the dose to one tablet daily for the first week to allow for lumacaftor's induction effect. After this period, resume the recommended daily dose. No dose adjustment is required for moderate or weak CYP3A4 inhibitors. 19. Grapefruit increases lumateperone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. If co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, limit the dose to 5 mg/day. 20. Grapefruit increases lumefantrine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 21. Grapefruit increases maraviroc levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 22. Grapefruit increases mavorixafor levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Reduce the daily dose when co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. 23. Grapefruit increases medroxyprogesterone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Use an alternative if available. 24. Grapefruit increases mefloquine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 25. Grapefruit increases mestranol levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 26. Grapefruit increases methadone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 27. Grapefruit increases methylprednisolone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 28. Grapefruit increases midazolam levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 29. Grapefruit increases mifepristone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 30. Grapefruit increases mirvetuximab soravtansine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase unconjugated DM4 exposure, raising the risk of adverse reactions. 31. Grapefruit increases naldemedine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism and P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor therapy. Monitor for potential adverse effects if co-administered with P-gp inhibitors. 32. Grapefruit increases nelfinavir levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 33. Grapefruit increases netupitant/palonosetron levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Netupitant is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4, but no dosage adjustment is required. 34. Grapefruit increases nicardipine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 35. Grapefruit increases nifedipine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Co-administration doubles nifedipine AUC and Cmax without altering its half-life. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking nifedipine. 36. Grapefruit increases nilotinib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 37. Grapefruit increases nintedanib levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. If adverse effects occur, management may require therapy interruption, dose reduction, or discontinuation. 38. Grapefruit increases nisoldipine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 39. Grapefruit increases norgestrel levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors may elevate systemic norgestrel concentrations, increasing the risk of adverse effects. 40. Grapefruit increases polatuzumab vedotin levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Polatuzumab undergoes catabolism to small peptides, amino acids, monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE), and unconjugated MMAE-related catabolites. MMAE is a CYP3A4 substrate. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase unconjugated MMAE AUC, raising the risk of toxicities. 41. Grapefruit increases praziquantel levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 42. Grapefruit increases prednisolone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 43. Grapefruit increases prednisone levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 44. Grapefruit increases propafenone levels by enhancing gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor therapy. 45. Grapefruit increases quazepam levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 46. Grapefruit increases quetiapine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 47. Grapefruit increases quinidine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 48. Grapefruit increases quizartinib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is recommended. Reduce the dose to 4 mg/day when co-administered with strong CYP3A inhibitors. If strong CYP3A inhibitors are discontinued, resume the pre-inhibitor dose after 5 half-lives. 49. Grapefruit increases red yeast rice levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. This may elevate creatine kinase levels and increase the risk of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis. Red yeast rice contains monacolin K, which is reportedly identical to lovastatin. 50. Grapefruit increases repaglinide levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 51. Grapefruit increases rifaximin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor therapy. 52. Grapefruit increases ripretinib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Co-administration with strong CYP3A inhibitors will increase systemic exposure to ripretinib and its active metabolite (DP-5439), raising the risk of adverse reactions. 53. Grapefruit increases ritonavir levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 54. Grapefruit increases rivaroxaban levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 55. Grapefruit increases romidepsin levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 56. Grapefruit increases seladelpar levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Exercise caution in patients who are poor CYP2C9 metabolizers and are co-administered a moderate/strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. 57. Grapefruit increases sertraline levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 58. Grapefruit increases sildenafil levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 59. Grapefruit increases solifenacin levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 60. Grapefruit increases sorafenib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 61. Grapefruit increases sufentanil SL levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Co-administration with CYP3A4 inhibitors may elevate sufentanil plasma concentrations, increasing or prolonging adverse effects, including potentially fatal respiratory depression. 62. Grapefruit increases sunitinib levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 63. Grapefruit increases tacrolimus levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 64. Grapefruit increases tadalafil levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 65. Grapefruit increases talazoparib levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor therapy. Talazoparib is a P-glycoprotein substrate; co-administration with P-gp inhibitors may elevate systemic exposure. 66. Grapefruit increases tamoxifen levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. CYP3A4 inhibition decreases tamoxifen metabolism to N-desmethyl tamoxifen, an active metabolite with similar biological activity. 67. Grapefruit increases tamsulosin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Dose reduction may be necessary for co-administered drugs predominantly metabolized by CYP3A. 68. Grapefruit increases temsirolimus levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 69. Grapefruit increases teniposide levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor therapy. 70. Grapefruit increases terbinafine levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 71. Grapefruit increases theophylline levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 72. Grapefruit increases ticagrelor levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 73. Grapefruit increases tinidazole levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 74. Grapefruit increases tipranavir levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. 75. Grapefruit increases tisotumab vedotin levels or effects by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor therapy. Its active metabolite (MMAE) is a CYP3A4 substrate. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase unconjugated MMAE systemic exposure, raising the risk of adverse reactions.
